summary: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
mainInsight: At every step the next output node is the smallest of the k current heads. A min-heap of heads gives that in O(log k); alternatively merge the lists pairwise in a divide-and-conquer fashion.

approaches.name: Merge one by one
approaches.summary: Fold lists into the result with a two-list merge.

approaches.name: Min-heap of heads
approaches.summary: Pop the smallest head, append it, push its next.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer pairwise merge
approaches.summary: Merge lists in pairs, halving the count each round.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal; divide-and-conquer merging achieves the same time with O(1) extra space.

promptVariants: Which structure gives the smallest of k list heads efficiently?
What pattern solves Merge k Sorted Lists in O(N log k)?
options: Min-heap of the current heads (or divide-and-conquer merging)
cards.answer: Min-heap of the current heads (or divide-and-conquer merging)
cards.explanation: The heap keeps k candidates; each pop/push is O(log k).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sorting all values only: Works in O(N log N) but ignores the sortedness and uses extra space.

promptVariants: Why does the heap need to hold only one node per list?
cards.answer: Each list is already sorted, so its smallest unmerged element is its current head. The global minimum is therefore among the k heads; after popping it, only that list's next node can become a new candidate and is pushed.
keyPoints: Head of each list = its minimum
Push only the popped node's next

promptVariants: Total time with N nodes and k lists: ___
Merge k Sorted Lists with a heap costs ___.
cards.explanation: N pops/pushes on a heap of size at most k.

promptVariants: What is the space cost of the heap solution versus divide and conquer?
cards.answer: Heap: O(k) for the heap entries. Divide and conquer merging reuses the nodes and needs O(1) extra (O(log k) if recursive).
cards.explanation: The output nodes are the existing nodes.

promptVariants: Why is `ListNode.__lt__` patched in your solution and what is a safer alternative?
What breaks if two nodes have the same value?
cards.code:
ListNode.__lt__ = lambda self, other: self.val < other.val
heap = [l for l in lists if l]
heapify(heap)
while heap:
    node = heappop(heap)
    cur.next = node
    cur = cur.next
    if node.next:
        heappush(heap, node.next)
cards.answer: heapq compares items with <, and ListNode defines no ordering, so the patch lets nodes be compared by value. Without it, equal values would fall back to comparing nodes and raise TypeError. A safer alternative is pushing (val, index, node) tuples where the unique index breaks ties.
cards.explanation: Mutating the class works in LeetCode but is a hack.

promptVariants: What does the code return for lists = [] or all empty lists?
options: None (nothing is pushed on the heap)
cards.answer: None (nothing is pushed on the heap)
cards.explanation: Only non-empty lists are pushed; an empty heap yields dummy.next = None.
